title: HeadRollback: Post-Task Attention Head Rollback for Replay-Free Continual LoRA Fine-Tuning

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in continual LoRA fine-tuning without relying on replay buffers or altered training. Papers [1], [2], [4], [5], [6], [12], and [28] all address catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, specifically in the context of LoRA or parameter-efficient fine-tuning. For example, [1] explicitly studies catastrophic forgetting in LoRA fine-tuning, while [5] discusses continual learning methods that avoid replay buffers. These papers share the same high-level objective of mitigating catastrophic forgetting in LoRA continual learning, even if the specific methods differ.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, HeadRollback, involves rolling back the LoRA B-matrix rows of disrupted attention heads to the previous checkpoint at task boundaries. Papers [9], [10], [13], [16], [18], and [26] discuss rollback mechanisms in various contexts, including checkpoint-based rollback recovery for distributed systems. For example, [9] introduces rollback mechanisms for session programming, and [10] describes checkpoint-based rollback recovery for message-passing systems. While these papers operate in different domains, the underlying primitive of rollback to a prior checkpoint is substantively equivalent to HeadRollback.

### Evaluation
The evaluation operates entirely at task boundaries with minimal state (one scalar per head plus a single checkpoint) but does not introduce a separate metric or benchmark for this contribution. Papers [1], [2], [4], [5], [6], [12], and [28] use similar evaluation designs for continual learning methods, including task-boundary-based interventions and checkpoint-based evaluations. For example, [5] evaluates continual LoRA methods at task boundaries, and [28] uses task-aware gated routing mechanisms evaluated across tasks. These designs match the evaluation framework of the contribution.

### Domain
The domain is continual learning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Papers [1], [2], [4], [5], [6], [12], and [28] all operate in the same general application area of continual learning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. For example, [1] and [4] focus on LoRA-based continual learning, while [12] emphasizes rehearsal-free continual learning methods. The contribution does not introduce a new application area but rather operates within this established domain.

Papers [1], [2], [4], [5], [8], [12] all address mitigating catastrophic forgetting in continual LoRA or parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings. The "without altered training" aspect is partially covered — most methods do alter training (regularization, orthogonality constraints), but the general purpose of replay-free catastrophic forgetting mitigation in continual LoRA is clearly covered by [2], [4], [12].

**MECHANISM: HeadRollback — a post-task intervention that rolls back LoRA B-matrix rows of unintentionally disrupted attention heads to the previous checkpoint at task boundaries.**

This is a selective, parameter-level rollback applied at task boundaries to specific attention heads identified as disrupted. Paper [29] ("Weights Reset Technique") resets random portions of layer weights periodically, but this is random and for regularization, not selective rollback of specific heads. Papers [9], [10], [13], [16], [18], [26], [27] all involve checkpoint-based rollback recovery, but these are in distributed computing/fault-tolerance contexts — the primitive of "roll back specific parameters to a previous checkpoint" is present, but the selectivity (identifying disrupted heads via a scalar criterion) is not. Paper [2] (I-LoRA) uses interpolation between checkpoints rather than rollback. No prior paper combines: (1) identifying specific attention heads as disrupted, (2) selectively rolling back only those heads' LoRA B-matrix rows, (3) as a post-task intervention without altering training. The closest is [29] (weight reset) but it's random, not selective. The checkpoint rollback papers [9],[10],[13],[16] use the rollback primitive but in entirely different contexts (fault tolerance) and without the head-selection criterion. The mechanism as a whole — selective head-level LoRA parameter rollback guided by a per-head scalar at task boundaries — appears genuinely absent.

This is a standard evaluation design used across the continual learning literature. The contribution is evaluated using the same benchmark family and metric semantics (accuracy/forgetting on sequential tasks) as papers [1], [2], [4], [8], [12].

**DOMAIN: Continual learning / parameter-efficient fine-tuning.**

Papers [1], [2], [4], [5], [8], [12] all operate in continual learning with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA specifically). This domain is clearly covered.

Both papers use the same evaluation design (benchmark-based validation of head importance scoring), making the evaluation covered.

The contribution operates in the domain of attention head importance scoring. Papers [4], [7], and [10] all work in the same general application area of attention head importance scoring in Transformers, even though they may target different specific tasks or datasets.
